metadata.name: Prism Dev Evaluation Set (12 papers)
metadata.domain: AI research papers (2026 preprints, arXiv 2610.*; mixed RL/distillation, agents, memory, benchmarking)
metadata.purpose: Development set for tuning the Prism auditor (e.g. thinking_level, model choice) before touching the frozen golden/held-out gates in matrix_eval.json and heldout_eval.json. Labelled under docs/LABEL_RUBRIC.md before any Prism output was read, then verified claim-by-claim against the source PDFs in docs/research_papers/. Golden labels in this file are frozen: do not relabel after seeing Prism output on these papers.
metadata.dev_set_size_rule: At least 30 independent refusal-family rows, amended from 40 BEFORE any Prism output was generated (docs/decisions.md, 'Dev set size rule amended - 2026-10-10'). This file has 32 refusal-family rows, but P8-R1/P8-R2 and P12-R1/P12-R2 each share their evidence base, so the independent count is about 30. Every reported result on this set must state the not_supported count (5 of 32) and flag that class as thin (margin roughly +/-17 points at a 45% refusal rate).

regression_gate.definition: Same four-bucket scoring as the golden set (refused / wrongly_affirmed / not_extracted / skipped) - see eval/scorer.py and docs/decisions.md. This file is not wired into CI; it is for offline experiment comparison (baseline vs thinking_level=high vs newer Flash), not a blocking gate.
regression_gate.run_policy: Do not relabel rows after seeing Prism's output on them. If a label turns out to be wrong on independent re-reading, log the correction in docs/decisions.md with a reason, do not silently edit this file to move the number.

label_counts.note: not_supported is a thin class (4 rows); treat any refusal-rate breakdown by label as low-confidence.

scoring_guidance.claim_matching: Actual engine rows are matched to expected rows via LLM-as-judge on claim_summary semantic equivalence - verbatim string match is not required.
scoring_guidance.evidence_matching: Fuzzy check: any expected_evidence_sections entry present in the actual row's evidence field counts as a match. Exact section-string identity not required.
scoring_guidance.label_matching: Exact match on the three-value vocabulary: supported | partially_supported | not_supported.

metadata.exact_quote_pass: Exact-quote pass 2026-10-10, before any Prism run: claim_text_verbatim replaced with exact PDF sentences; rows dropped for having no single-sentence source: P11-S5, P3-S3, P5-S8, P6-S6, P6-S7, P7-S7, P9-S5.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Removing either baseline, replacing the residual by the log ratio, or adding direct supervision of the teacher's top token lowers performance.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Every tested ablation variant (removing a baseline, using the log-ratio form, or adding direct top-token supervision) reduces performance relative to full RA.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 4: adding the branch to sampled OPD raises Avg +0.30 and Pass +0.64, contradicting the blanket 'lowers performance' claim for that one ablation variant.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Cell-by-cell check (R3) catches one ablation cell that improves rather than lowers performance.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The guidance term decreases both as the student approaches the teacher and as the student becomes confident in its own choice, an elegant property that helps RA preserve exploration in RL.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The residual-advantage mechanism has a demonstrated property of preserving RL exploration.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: No exploration measure appears anywhere in the paper; Section 4.4 itself frames the mechanism as a conjecture, not a measured property. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested mechanism claim (R1/R5): the hedge 'helps preserve' does not rescue a property that is never measured.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The second bounds the guidance amplitude by the student–teacher distance on the visited prefixes (Appendix A.6), so teacher guidance fades as the two converge, at a fixed weight and without a schedule; Appendix C.1 shows the mean absolute guidance declining over a training run.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The RA guidance term shrinks as the student model's performance approaches the teacher's during training.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Single seed, single 4B run; Appendix A.6/A.9 state that the reported bounds do not actually show how guidance evolves over training. Judgment call. Related sentences (not the claim): The guidance term decreases both as the student approaches the teacher and as the student becomes confident in its own choice, an elegant property that helps RA preserve exploration in RL. (p.9).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Scope limited to one seed/one model size (R3); the paper's own appendix disclaims that the bound demonstrates the dynamic being claimed.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across two students, two estimators, and three mathematical benchmarks, RA improves all 24 three-seed benchmark means of its base estimator, both combinations surpass teacher-only OPD, and Co-RA raises accuracy further with mixed changes in coverage.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: RA improves over the base algorithm in every one of 24 tested comparisons.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: All 24 pairwise comparisons increase (checked cell by cell, R3).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: With Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base students and a Qwen3-8B teacher, RA combined with GRPO or REINFORCE++ improves the underlying sequence-advantage algorithm in all 24 comparisons on three mathematical benchmarks, raising macro Avg@8 by 1.7–3.6 points and Pass@8 by 3.9–6.3 points.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: RA's macro-averaged gains range 1.7-3.6 points on Avg@8 and 3.9-6.3 points on Pass@8.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Both combinations surpass teacher-only OPD, and Co-RA adds a further 1.0–1.5 Avg@8 points.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Adding Co-RA on top of RA yields a further 1.0-1.5 point gain on Avg@8.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Co-RA adds 1.03–1.45 macro Avg@8 points to the four RA runs, and Avg@8 rises in all twelve benchmark means.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Adding Co-RA raises the Avg@8 mean in all twelve tested configurations.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 12 of 12 cells rise.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: From K = 8 to K = 512 for the 1.7B REINFORCE++ runs (Appendix D.7), the macro margin of RA over the untrained student grows from 13.4 to 16.9 points, and its margins over REINFORCE++ and OPD from 5.8 to 10.4 and from 3.9 to 6.8, while that of verifier-only training narrows from 7.6 to 6.6, as Yue et al. (2025) report for RLVR.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The Pass@512 margin between RA and the untrained student grows from 13.4 to 16.9 points.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Every residual variant improves on verifier-only training at every tested weight, and full RA stays above every control at every matched weight.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: All residual variants outperform verifier-only training, and full RA beats every control at matched weight.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: All columns checked.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The probability residual with both baselines is the best construction, and no log-ratio variant reaches it at any swept weight.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: No tested log-ratio variant of the method matches the performance of full RA.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Best log variant 28.04/43.50, below full RA 29.25/45.20.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Yet each adapted teacher scores 0.8–2.3 macro Avg@8 and 0.7–3.5 Pass@8 points below the frozen teacher (Appendix D.9), while the students it guides improve: it is a better guide, not a better solver.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The adapted teacher model is a worse solver than the unadapted teacher by 0.8-2.3 points Avg and 0.7-3.5 points Pass.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On the 256 offline responses of Appendix C.2, the local advantages average to 3 × 10−4 per token, so the student value baseline leaves no systematic part, and on responses longer than 1,000 tokens the shift has an SD below 0.03, where centering changes almost nothing (Proposition 4).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The paper reports a per-token average local advantage of 3x10^-4.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 16 reports the mean over responses (+0.03 = 0.003 per token), a different measurement from the token-pooled mean the text states, so no conflict under the same-measurement check (R4).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Two numbers for what looks like one baseline, resolved via R4: different measurement units, not a contradiction.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: In principle, the same inference-time approach could be applied to a model fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RLFT) by providing its response as context to the parent model.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The SFT-as-context approach can naturally be extended to models fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL-as-context).
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Never tested; Appendix E explicitly states 'we do not apply SFT-as-context (or RL-as-context)'. Related sentences (not the claim): Since the same framework could naturally extend beyond SFT to other post-training methods, such as reinforcement learning, we leave this as a promising future direction to combine capabilities acquired through post-training with the broad capabilities of pretrained models. (p.10).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested generalization claim (R1+R5): 'in principle'/'could naturally extend' hedges do not rescue a mechanism the paper never runs.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: SFT-as-context incurs modest overhead compared with SFT.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Using SFT-as-context at inference time adds only modest computational overhead relative to plain SFT.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: NutriBench-English overhead is 198.1%, Non-English 143.9% - clearly not 'modest'. Body text calls nutrition an outlier, but the table title (the claim as worded) does not carve this out. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): a title-level 'modest overhead' claim is contradicted by specific cells the body text itself flags as outliers but the title does not exclude.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: RL-trained models do not show forgetting of instruction-following capability compared to their parent, as measured by IFEval.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Models fine-tuned with RL show no forgetting of instruction-following ability.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Average delta is -0.22, but individual models drop substantially: FastCuRL-1.5B-Preview -3.51, Skywork-OR1-Math-7B -3.14, AceMath-RL-Nemotron-7B -2.03, Polaris-7B-Preview -2.03. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): an aggregate 'no forgetting' caption masks individually large per-model drops.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: As shown in Tables 7 and 8, SFT-as-context outperforms even the oracle router.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: SFT-as-context beats the oracle router baseline across all tested model pairs.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 7: Bespoke-Stratos-7B ties (0.0) rather than winning. Table 8: OlympicCoder-7B is -1.9 (a loss). The Table 8 caption names this exception itself, so that caption is separately supported; the quoted sentence as worded is not. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): 'outperforms even the oracle router' as a blanket claim is contradicted by a tie and a loss cell.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across 19 parent-SFT model pairs and 11 benchmarks, SFT-as-context remains close to the SFT models on fine-tuned capabilities, with gaps of only 2.2 and 2.1 percentage points on AIME 2024 and LiveCodeBench and 2.0 macro MAE on NutriBench-English, while staying within 2.2 percentage points of the parent models on general capabilities on average.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: On average, SFT-as-context stays within 2.2 points of the parent model's general-capability scores.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: 11 general-capability gaps average 1.86 (aggregate claim). First half (former P2-S1): Table 1: 56.0-53.8, 55.5-53.4, 18.4-16.4

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Using SFT checkpoints collected from Hugging Face, SFT-as-context achieves 95.0% and 94.1% recovery rates of the fine-tuning gains on AIME 2024 and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), respectively.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: SFT-as-context recovers 95.0% of the SFT gain on AIME 2024, 94.1% on LiveCodeBench, and 94.2% average on general capabilities.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1 'Recovery' column; 1036.5/11 = 94.2.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: As shown in Table 1, SFT causes substantial forgetting of general capabilities, reducing general capability scores by 33.2 percentage points on average.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Plain SFT reduces general-capability scores by 33.2 points on average relative to the parent model.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: 11 gaps sum to 364.9, mean 33.17.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: For example, among the three nutrition SFT models, Qwen3-8B shows the largest drop in acknowledging non-food queries, from 99.6% to 10.7%, catastrophically forgetting the instruction-following capability of its parent model.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Qwen3-8B shows the largest drop in correctly flagging non-food inputs, from 99.6% to 10.7%.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Figure 2(c): -88.9, the largest drop of the three models shown.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: This is effectively mitigated by a larger parent: the 32B parent exhibits this failure far less often, yielding a smaller remaining gap for the 32B models than for the 7B ones (an average gap of −1.8 versus −7.5).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The gap left by SFT-as-context is smaller for the 32B model than the 7B model: -1.8 vs -7.5 points average.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: As shown in Table 2, using responses from open-source SFT models as context consistently improves the performance of a strong proprietary model on NutriBench-English, achieving lower MAE than either model alone.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Using an open-source model's SFT trace as context consistently improves a strong proprietary model's NutriBench-English score.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 2: all 3 tested contexts (14.13, 14.08, 14.41) beat Gemini alone (17.44); checked cell by cell (R3).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Specifically, the ratio of second-pass to first-pass response tokens is at most 13.0%.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The fraction of cases needing a second generation pass is at most 13.0% for math and coding tasks.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 10: max 13.0 (IFEval, math); all other math and coding rows lower.

papers.title: JevKT: When Few or No Learners Are Logged?

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Among the readers we tested, the gain comes from the model rather than the typed format; the input recipe helps other LLMs as much as it helps Jev.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The JevKT input-format recipe helps any LLM reader by about the same amount, not just the Jev model.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Only one other LLM (DeepSeek) was run with the JevKT input; GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite have no N=8 results (Table 2). Gains are +.016 (Jev) vs +.010 (DeepSeek) - 'never differ significantly' is not the same as 'helps as much'.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss / scope row (R3): 'as much as' overstates a result measured on a single alternate model with a smaller gain.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: For new learners the advantage holds from their first interactions, whereas on unseen items with all learners logged, deep KT remains ahead.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: JevKT's advantage over deep knowledge-tracing baselines is present even at a new learner's very first interactions.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 9 position 1: JevKT loses to best deep KT on A09 (.709 vs .749) and XES3G5M (.512 vs .542); Jev0-shot is below best deep KT on the mean (.580 vs .605). The paper itself calls position 1 'noisy' and starts its own counts at position 2. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the claimed advantage at the very first interaction is contradicted by the paper's own position-1 numbers.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Without any data from the target platform, Jev0-shot reaches .706 mean AUC (first block of Table 1).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Jev0-shot's mean AUC of .706 beats both LOKT (.671) and the best deep knowledge-tracing model trained on 8 learners (.689), winning on 5 of 7 datasets.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1 values as stated; Jev loses on DBE (.742 vs .793) and Alg05 (.698 vs .711), consistent with 5/7.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Core headline comparison, verified cell by cell.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: JevKT is ahead of the best deep KT model by +.033, +.023 and +.016 mean AUC at N=8, 16 and 32 (on 7/7, 7/7 and 7/7 datasets); the mean difference is +.004 at N=64, −.002 at N=128, −.008 at N=256 and −.028 with the full training data.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: JevKT beats the best deep KT baseline on all 7 datasets at each of N=8, 16, and 32 learners, by margins of +.033, +.023, +.016.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: A reasoning budget of 1024 or 2048 tokens never improves AUC significantly over the same model without reasoning, while one Jev pass beats Thinking-KT on all seven datasets (Holm-corrected, ∆AUC +.038 to +.073 against the budget of 2048).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: A single Jev pass beats the Thinking-KT baseline on all 7 datasets, with Holm-corrected gains of +.038 to +.073.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: All seven values positive and marked significant in Table 3.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: One JevKT prediction takes 325 ms in a single call and costs $886 per million predictions, about 1/5 of Thinking-KT, which needs $4,360 and 41.7 s per prediction even with its ten votes issued in parallel; Jev0-shot costs $44.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Jev0-shot costs about 1/100th and JevKT about 1/5th of Thinking-KT's per-million-prediction cost ($4,360).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: At N=16 the similar-learner statistic alone raises Jev0-shot from .706 to .729, 64 KC-matched shots alone to .724, and both together to .730.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: At N=16, the similar-learner statistic accounts for almost all of the improvement over the few-shot examples component.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Quoted figures match the text and Table 6.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: JevKT (.713) and Jev0-shot (.704) stay well above LOKT (.664), but the best deep KT model, trained on all learners and chosen on test, is ahead (.729; JevKT is better on 1/7 datasets; Table 10).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: On unseen items with the full learner log available, the best deep KT baseline beats JevKT on average and on 6 of 7 datasets.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Figure 3b and Table 10 confirm the disclosed loss.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across multiple sparse baselines, benchmarks, and LLM backbones, MASA gives consistent gains under matched settings with negligible latency overhead.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA consistently improves accuracy over baseline sparse-attention methods under matched settings.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: MInference at 64K drops 82.3 -> 81.57; FlexPrefill-Qwen at 8K drops 89.91 -> 88.94. Table 2: MInference En.Sum drops 20.5 -> 19.73, En.QA 12.9 -> 12.15; FlexPrefill-Llama En.MC drops 69.43 -> 66.81. The paper's own body text says '11 of 12', but the abstract/conclusion wording does not carve out these losses. Related sentences (not the claim): Under matched settings with the original baselines, MASA gives consistent accuracy gains, supporting both the proposed method and the matrix-approximation view of sparse attention. (p.2).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): a headline 'consistent gains' claim is contradicted by several measured regressions the body text acknowledges but the headline does not.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Norm clipping is helpful for SeerAttention and FlexPrefill-Llama, while soft norm balancing is useful in some FlexPrefill settings.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Norm clipping reliably helps SeerAttention and FlexPrefill-Llama.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: FlexPrefill-Llama has no raw MASA result in Tables 9/10, so 'helpful' was never actually measured against a raw baseline for it. For SeerAttention on RULER, clip-85 (87.76) and clip-95 (87.79) are both below raw (87.88); only clip-90 (88.09) helps.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested/hidden-loss combination (R3/R5): one half of the claim lacks the comparison it needs, and the other half only partially holds across clip settings.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: MASA does not change the sparse kernels, candidate sparse units, or budget rules of existing methods, making it orthogonal to low-level attention kernels and other LLM acceleration techniques as discussed in Appendix A.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA is orthogonal to (compatible with) other LLM acceleration techniques beyond the sparse-attention kernels it was tested with.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: The kernel side is well exercised (three frameworks, official kernels), but MASA is never combined with any other acceleration technique; Appendix A argues orthogonality by design only, not by experiment. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested generalization claim (R5): compatibility with 'other LLM acceleration techniques' broadly is argued by design, not demonstrated.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: MASA improves all eight matched average scores across three sparse methods, three benchmark suites, and both Llama- and Qwen-family backbones.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA improves the average score in all 8 matched method/benchmark/backbone combinations.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across the four RULER configurations at 32K, 64K, and 128K, MASA improves 11 of 12 matched length-level scores.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA improves 11 of the 12 matched RULER length-level scores at 32K/64K/128K.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: the only loss is MInference at 64K.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: For every configuration, the mean gain over these longer contexts at 32K–128K exceeds that at 4K–16K.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA's gains are consistently larger at longer context lengths (32K-128K) than at shorter lengths (4K-16K).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: At 128K, MASA improves MInference, SeerAttention, FlexPrefill-Llama, and FlexPrefill-Qwen by 1.28, 0.48, 1.45, and 2.16 points, respectively.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA's largest RULER gains occur at 128K and 64K context lengths across the tested methods.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Verified against Table 1 columns. Related sentences (not the claim): At 64K, the gains reach 2.16 points for FlexPrefill-Llama and 3.65 points for FlexPrefill-Qwen. (p.8).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On InfiniteBench, MASA raises FlexPrefill-Llama from 47.14 to 47.99 against a full-attention score of 48.06, recovering approximately 92% of the original average-score deficit.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA recovers about 92% of FlexPrefill-Llama's InfiniteBench deficit relative to full attention.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 2: deficit .92, recovered .85, i.e. 92.4%.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On RULER, MASA raises SeerAttention from 87.60 to 88.09, moving it from below the dense reference to above it.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA moves SeerAttention's RULER score from below the dense-attention reference to above it.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: dense reference is 88.01.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: For FlexPrefill-Llama on RULER, replacing the ranking score adds 0.76 points, exceeding the original method’s 0.48-point advantage over full attention and increasing that advantage to 1.24 points.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA increases FlexPrefill-Llama's RULER advantage over full attention from 0.48 to 1.24 points.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Attention-output error decreases across all four evaluated framework–backbone pairs.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MASA lowers attention-output error for every tested framework-backbone pair, with all confidence intervals excluding zero.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Confirmed in Table 8; note the paper itself scopes this to 64K RULER and 8 prespecified layers, and calls the intervals selected-setting comparisons.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Cell-by-cell check (R3), with the paper's own scope note preserved.

papers.title: Semi-OPD: When Do We Need On-Policy Distillation?

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The gains transfer beyond the training domain.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Semi-OPD's gains generalize beyond the math domain it was trained on, to broader reasoning tasks.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Figure 11 caption shows only one student-teacher pair (Qwen3-1.7B <- Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507), tested on coding only (HumanEval, HumanEval+). Every other pair is trained and evaluated only on DAPO-Math. Related sentences (not the claim): This suggests that the gains are not limited to fitting the math training distribution but transfer to broader reasoning tasks. (p.8).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested generalization claim (R5): a broad transfer claim rests on a single pair tested on a single off-domain benchmark family.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: We evaluate across 17 teacher–student pairs spanning 1.5B to 235B parameters and three model families in both thinking and non-thinking modes, covering the most commonly used student–teacher pairs in the OPD literature.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The paper's 17 model pairs cover the most commonly used student-teacher combinations in the OPD literature.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 3 rows g and h are SFT-warm-started variants of pairs a and f, so there are really 15 distinct pairs, not 17; one training domain (math); no survey evidence is given for 'most commonly used'. The SFT variants are disclosed in Section 2.1. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Scope/count overclaim (R5): 'most commonly used' is an unsupported comparative framing, and the pair count double-counts two SFT variants.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: This cannot be addressed by simple truncation, as we empirically show the importance of covering supervision signals from different reasoning stages.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Truncating the training signal to fewer tokens cannot match Semi-OPD's coverage of different reasoning stages.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: FastOPD (4K truncation) beats Standard OPD by +4.5 (1.7B: 30.7 vs 26.2) and +7.6 (4B: 52.5 vs 44.9), and beats Semi-OPD on Cascade-2 (74.8 vs 74.1); it trails Semi-OPD only at low overlap. Judgment call.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the blanket 'cannot be addressed by truncation' claim is contradicted by cases where truncation (FastOPD) matches or beats Semi-OPD.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across 17 teacher–student pairs ranging from 1.5B to 235B parameters, Semi-OPD outperforms OPD in 14 cases, with up to +13.6% accuracy and 11.4× training speedup.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Semi-OPD beats standard OPD on 14 of 17 model pairs, with gains up to 13.6 points.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1: 39.8 vs 26.2; Table 3: 14 pairs with positive last-step gain.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On the remaining three pairs, Semi-OPD still achieves comparable performance, with gaps of 0.1–2.6%.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: On the 3 pairs where Semi-OPD doesn't win, it is close behind, within 0.1-2.6 points.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 3 last-step: -0.1 (Cascade-2), -1.7 (R1-Distill-7B <- Light-R1), -2.6 (R1-Distill-7B <- Polaris).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Semi-OPD outperforms standard OPD when the initial teacher–student overlap is low.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Semi-OPD's advantage over standard OPD is strongest when teacher-student overlap is low.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 3: all 11 pairs with overlap < 70% have positive AUC gain (+0.24 to +7.57).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The two quantities are strongly correlated (Pearson’s 𝑟= −0.73 across 17 pairs): pairs with lower initial overlap ratios tend to benefit substantially more from Semi-OPD, while OPD is only needed for pairs with high overlap ratios.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: There's a strong negative correlation (r=-0.73) between Semi-OPD's gain over OPD and initial teacher-student overlap.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Recomputed from Table 3: r = -0.735 (AUC gain); -0.78 without the two SFT-variant pairs.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: We observe that (1) on the Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and Qwen3-4B (non-thinking) students, which have low teacher–student overlap ratios, Semi-OPD outperforms all other baselines in accuracy while also being the most efficient, e.g., achieving +7.1% and +8.8% higher accuracy with 35× and 19.5× less training time than Relay-OPD on the two pairs, respectively, according to Fig. 1 and Tab. 4.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Semi-OPD beats Relay-OPD on accuracy while using far less training time, on both the 1.7B and 4B Qwen3 models.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On the Nemotron-Cascade-2 pair, which has a high overlap ratio of approximately 89%, our Semi-OPD remains competitive with other OPD baselines and falls only slightly behind the best baseline by 0.7% accuracy, while reducing the training time by 2.2x as compared to FastOPD and 4.5x compared to OPD.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: On the highest-overlap pair, Semi-OPD trades a small accuracy loss for a large training-time reduction.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification of a self-disclosed negative result.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The overall accuracy–training-efficiency trade-off is shown in Fig. 1, where Semi-OPD achieves up to an 11.4× speedup over standard OPD and a 2.7× speedup over the fastest baseline, FastOPD.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Semi-OPD's maximum speedup is 11.4x over standard OPD and 2.7x over the fastest baseline, FastOPD.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: These results establish constrained compilation as a scalable and auditable framework for medical VLM benchmark construction beyond question generation.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The constrained-compilation framework is a scalable, auditable solution for building medical VLM benchmarks beyond just generating questions.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Only two domains tested (breast imaging: 3 datasets; dermoscopy: 1 dataset). Planning checkpoints use researcher review (Section 5.1); Limitations state 'limited human involvement remains at planning checkpoints'. No scaling, throughput, cost, or time measurement appears anywhere. 'Auditable' is backed (994/1,000 audit pass rate); 'scalable ... beyond question generation' is not tested.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested generalization claim (R3/scope): 'scalable' is asserted without any scaling measurement; the audited part of the claim is separable and does hold.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: We further demonstrate portability to a specialized medical domain and evaluate twelve VLMs, revealing task- and setting-specific variation obscured by aggregate scores.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The framework was shown to port to a specialized medical domain, and 12 VLMs were evaluated there.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 3 (breast imaging) lists 12 VLMs. Table 10 (ISIC 2018 dermoscopy, the specialized domain referenced) lists only 11: BreastGPT-8B is absent. Main-text Figure 3 shows only 8 models. Scope ambiguity: 'resulting benchmark' could instead refer to the breast benchmark, where 12 is correct.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the '12 VLMs' count does not hold for the dermoscopy table specifically, though it does for the breast-imaging table.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: MedBenchAgent achieves a Task-Space F1 of 90.9%, outperforming direct task induction (79.2–80.0%) and prior-guided induction (85.1%); 994 of 1,000 sampled items from correctly identified tasks pass human audit.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MedBenchAgent's Task-Space F1 of 90.9% beats direct induction (79.2-80.0%) and prior-guided induction (85.1%).
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Values as stated in Table 1.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Table 2 shows that 994 items pass, yielding a 99.4% consistency rate.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Human audit passes 994 of 1,000 sampled benchmark items (99.4%).
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 994 pass, 6 fail (4 VinDr BI-RADS finding-type, 2 BrEaST unsupported additions).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Providing T0 improves direct DeepSeek-V4-Flash induction to 85.1% F1, while MedBenchAgent further increases precision from 76.9% to 87.0% at the same 95.2% recall, reducing false positives from six to three.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: MedBenchAgent raises precision from 76.9% to 87.0% at matched recall, halving false positives relative to giving the model T0 directly.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Precision/recall/FP values consistent with TP=20, FN=1.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: All methods achieve 100% EMA on matched tasks.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Every method tested reaches 100% exact-match accuracy on matched tasks.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Checked cell by cell: all five rows read 100.0%.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: As shown in Table 3, medical VLMs outperform general-purpose VLMs by 6.23 points in Overall Acc. but trail by 2.48 points on AC, indicating that the aggregate advantage is not uniform across tasks.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Medical-specialized VLMs beat general-purpose VLMs on overall accuracy, but lose on the AC metric.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: FA improves by 27.09 points, while AA, FT, AC, DX, and PS decrease by 9.37, 1.22, 0.53, 4.85, and 7.50 points, respectively.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Enabling 'thinking' mode on Qwen3-VL-8B helps FA sharply but hurts five other metrics.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: These observations demonstrate substantial resource savings in noisy tool-use trajectories and identify workload dependence as a central consideration for reversible context management.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The method demonstrates substantial resource savings across noisy tool-use trajectories.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Plural 'trajectories' rests on one OpenTelemetry pair (Table 1). Section 7 states 'one OpenTelemetry pair and one Planroom pair do not estimate the variance of the policy's effect' and calls it 'a development-informed case study rather than a held-out confirmatory benchmark'. The retained arm also had 275 logical image occurrences vs none for the method arm, so the saving cannot be attributed to text archival alone. Judgment call - an alternate reading treats this as supported since the abstract itself carves out workload dependence via the Planroom case.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Scope-of-generalization row (R3): a plural, generalized savings claim rests on a single confounded case study.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: In principle, the same contract can cover documentation, diagnostic logs, browser text, and images.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The archival contract can in principle cover documentation, diagnostic logs, browser text, and images.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Documentation (Planroom, Context7), diagnostic logs and browser text (OpenTelemetry) were actually archived and tested. Section 5.3 states 'no image payload is archived'. The 'in principle' hedge narrows scope but does not rescue the untested image modality.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested modality (R1): the hedge narrows but does not fully rescue an untested claim about images specifically.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: In an exploratory OpenTelemetry debugging case followed by an unrelated implementation task, the method ended with 231,951 provider-reported prompt tokens versus 912,492 under retained history, used 50% fewer cumulative input tokens, and had an estimated API cost of $1.28–$1.44 versus approximately $4.38.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The method roughly quarters the final prompt size and halves cumulative input tokens, cutting cost from ~$4.38 to $1.28-$1.44.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Both arms passed the two-case primary behavioral oracle; neither fully satisfied the follow-up evaluation.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Both the method and retained-context arms passed the primary test oracle but failed to fully satisfy the follow-up test.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 2/2 vs 2/2 on the primary oracle; follow-up 3/6 vs 2/6.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification of a disclosed limitation.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The method made more requests and took 17% longer.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The archival method is slower and makes more requests than the retained-context baseline, despite lower token cost.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 185 vs 121 requests; 2,025 vs 1,730 s = +17.05%; 71,919 vs 33,834 completion tokens = 2.126x. Related sentences (not the claim): method generates more than twice as many completion tokens and takes 17% longer. (p.8).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification of a disclosed trade-off.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: At primary submission the method carries 124,746 prompt tokens versus 847,674 for retained, an 85% reduction.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The method cuts prompt size by about 85% at primary submission and 75% at the final step.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: -85.28%; -74.58%. Related sentences (not the claim): After the follow-up, the method carries 231,951 versus 912,492 prompt tokens, a 75% reduction. (p.7).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The estimated cost is approximately 67–71% lower, even after reported cache usage is included.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The method's estimated cost is roughly 67-71% lower than the retained-context baseline.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The method therefore shows stronger tested signal handling but weaker tested startup-failure handling.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The method handles process signals better than the baseline, but handles startup failures worse.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Method exits 0 after SIGTERM (8.43s) and SIGINT (8.85s); retained is killed with 137. Retained passes the occupied-port probe (status 1); method's second process times out at 30s.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric/behavioral verification of a disclosed trade-off.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Every method session has a smaller final prompt than every retained session, while cumulative usage overlaps.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The method always ends with a smaller final prompt than the baseline, even though total token usage across sessions overlaps.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Max method final 145,213 < min retained final 234,057 (checked cell by cell, R3). Totals overlap: method 8.29M-16.85M vs retained 12.27M-20.22M.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Concurrently, a recursive prefix consolidation mechanism repeatedly consolidates earlier history, causing long-unused experiences to become increasingly abstract.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Unused experiences and knowledge items progressively lose detail over time through recursive consolidation.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 10 (ToolBench knowledge-item transitions) shows 'No detected use' items are 95.8% unchanged, only 3.1% rewritten and 0.1% dropped. Appendix A.6 itself states these statistics 'do not establish general fading of unused knowledge'. The PALIM Step 3 prompt states consolidated knowledge 'survives every later fold... nothing is shortened out of it'. Narrative does get coarser by fold age (Fig. 7), but that was never measured against use/disuse specifically. Shares evidence with P8-R2. Related sentences (not the claim): Experience that remains unused continues to recede in detail through recursive consolidation, without separately assigned importance scores or time-based forgetting rules. (p.2); In contrast, incidental details and knowledge not currently used are retained in progressively less detail through recursive Prefix Consolidation, reducing their interference with ongoing reasoning and decisions. (p.5).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the paper's own appendix disclaims that its data establishes the claimed disuse-driven fading for knowledge items.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: These results demonstrate how our use-and-disuse cycle supports memory and learning through interaction history.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The experiments demonstrate both the 'use' and 'disuse' halves of the memory cycle.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: The 'use' half is backed: used items are supplemented 28.4% (call matches) and 11.7% (call differs) of the time vs 0.9% with no detected use. The 'disuse' half is not demonstrated, per the same Appendix A.6 concession as P8-R1; the use proxy is also only API-linked, not shown to directly influence reasoning. Shares evidence with P8-R1. Related sentences (not the claim): Experiments and analyses demonstrate its broad applicability and illuminate how retained knowledge evolves through use and disuse. (p.9).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the 'use' half of a compound claim is supported, the 'disuse' half is not.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: These gains demonstrate more effective learning from accumulated experience than the compared methods.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Hippocam learns more effectively from accumulated experience than all the methods it is compared against.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: The sentence follows Figure 4, which tracks only the three leading methods per StreamBench stream to task 300. In Table 1 (same RQ1 section), ACE (91.9) and A-Mem (87.2) beat Hippocam (81.9) on ScienceWorld. The ToolBench lead over Letta at 300 tasks is only 78.7 vs 77.3. Judgment call - an alternate reading restricts 'the compared methods' to the Figure 4 subset only.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): 'than the compared methods' reads as all baselines, but two baselines beat Hippocam on the same table.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across the three benchmarks, most methods outperform Plain, although some match or fall below it.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Most memory methods beat a no-memory baseline across the three benchmarks, with a few exceptions.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Plain 78.4/66.9/69.0. 16 of 21 baseline cells above Plain, 2 equal (ReasoningBank SciWorld 66.9; HiAgent StreamBench 69.0), 3 below (HiAgent 56.7, mem0 58.6 on SciWorld; ReasoningBank 68.3 on StreamBench).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Its 81.9% mean ScienceWorld progress exceeds four of the six compared methods.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Hippocam's ScienceWorld score beats 4 of the 6 other memory methods tested.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Exceeds HiAgent 56.7, mem0 58.6, Letta 71.2, ReasoningBank 66.9; trails A-Mem 87.2 and ACE 91.9.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification including the disclosed losses.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On StreamBench, it achieves the highest mean accuracy of 81.7%, narrowly ahead of Letta's 81.3%.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Hippocam is the top performer on StreamBench, barely ahead of Letta.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Hippocam 81.7; Letta 81.3; next-best A-Mem 79.0.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Hippocam achieves 78.9% mean progress, improving over Plain by 30.1 pp and exceeding the strongest baseline, ACE, by 16.2 pp.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: On a different benchmark, Hippocam beats both the no-memory baseline (+30.1) and the strongest competitor ACE (+16.2).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: On FEVER, Frozen scores cluster around Plain's 59.3%, with Hippocam and HiAgent reaching 61.8%.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: On FEVER, most frozen-memory methods score near the no-memory baseline, with Hippocam and HiAgent tied for the top score.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: HiAgent 61.8, mem0 59.9, Letta 59.9, ACE 57.9, A-Mem 55.8, ReasoningBank 55.8, Hippocam 61.8.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Only Hippocam and ACE achieve positive gains on both domain transitions, while the remaining methods show mixed, unchanged, or reduced performance.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Of all methods tested, only Hippocam and ACE improve on both cross-domain transfer settings.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Delta-stream (Sci, FEVER): Hippocam +19.2/+6.0; ACE +14.0/+2.0; HiAgent +0.1/-5.8; mem0 -28.1/0.0; A-Mem -8.0/0.0; Letta -4.8/-9.9; ReasoningBank -11.2/-2.1.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Prefix consolidation thus supports more effective subsequent work with a smaller active context.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Consolidating the prefix lets later work proceed with a smaller active context while staying effective.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: ToolBench 78.7 vs 65.7; ALFWorld steps 9.62 vs 11.74; context 19.7k vs 50.7k. The text itself carves out the one loss: ALFWorld success 97.8 vs 100.0, calling it 'remains near perfect'.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Disabling recall on the same post-ingestion MemoryAgentBench 64k snapshot reduces accuracy from 41.0% to 27.0%.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Removing the recall mechanism drops accuracy substantially, showing the consolidated context alone is not sufficient.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 41.0 vs 27.0 on the same post-ingestion snapshot.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Third, LinUOT tracks OnTrack within 0.003–0.010 AUROC everywhere: the quadratic term contributes essentially nothing to ranking on this corpus, consistent with its role as a false-alarm suppressor rather than a ranker (Table 4); the mask-free variant is AUROC-identical to the full system, confirming the mask’s null ranking effect here as well.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The simpler LinUOT variant tracks full OnTrack within 0.003-0.010 AUROC at every tested k.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 5, OnTrack vs LinUOT: k=5 .612 vs .595 (gap .017); k=8 .631 vs .628 (.003); k=10 .622 vs .614 (.008); k=15 .635 vs .626 (.009); k=20 .648 vs .638 (.010). 'Everywhere' breaks at k=5, where the gap (.017) exceeds the stated .010 ceiling; the other four points fit. The gap is small throughout, so the main point (the quadratic term adds little to ranking) still stands.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Cell-by-cell check (R3): one of five k-values exceeds the stated bound, breaking the literal 'everywhere' claim while leaving the substance intact.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Evaluating based on the first 8 steps, the proposed method ranked the failing trajectories below succeeding ones better than content similarity-based approaches (+0.057 AUROC).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: At k=8, OnTrack beats a cosine-similarity baseline at distinguishing failing from succeeding trajectories by 0.057 AUROC.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: OnTrack .631, cosine .574, delta +.057 [.033, .080].

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: First, the ∆CI excludes zero at k ≤10, and the advantage is gone by k=15, where cosine catches up (.633 vs. .635): the claim is an early-trajectory advantage, precisely the regime an in-flight monitor operates in.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: OnTrack's advantage over cosine is statistically significant up to k=10 but disappears by k=15.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Second, at the shipped threshold the quadratic structure term selects a lower-FPR operating point: removing the mask changes almost nothing (13/40 →14/40 false-positive traces at essentially identical recall), while removing the GW term more than doubles the benign false-alarm count (29/40), to nearly the level of running no transport at all (L1-only 31/40, rule baseline 32/40).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Ablating the GW term roughly doubles the false-alarm count, while ablating the mask barely changes it.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 29/40 > 2 x 13/40 = 26/40; counts as stated.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Additionally, by deploying an abort policy on top of it, we save ∼18% of the compute that would have been burned on agents heading to failure, and 83% of runs that were interrupted were actually heading to failure (5 out of every 6 aborts were correct).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: An abort threshold of 0.60 saves roughly 18% of compute while keeping 83% precision.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Cost saved 17.9%; precision 83%; true stop 23.3%, false stop 20.7% (n=150 per class, balanced). Threshold selection disclosed as a candidate policy, not calibrated on held-out data.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification with a disclosed methodological caveat preserved.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Beyond the eight unit scenarios, a randomized campaign (40 random-DAG tasks × 7 conditions, seeded) yields: loop recall 100% at detection latency 0; hallucination recall 100% at latency 2 (the grace window); causal-inversion recall 94.1% at latency 0 via the premature-step check; and 0 false interventions over 200 benign runs that include valid reorderings, retries, and parallel exploration (a one-sided 95% upper bound of 1.5% on the false-intervention rate).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: A randomized campaign shows perfect or near-perfect detection recall for several failure types with zero false interventions on benign runs.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: As stated in the text (40 random-DAG tasks x 7 conditions, seeded).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Measured on an Apple M5 Max core, the fast path runs at p50 0.85 ms / p95 1.6 ms per event at t=m=40, K=3 (p50 0.5 / p95 0.7 ms at t=m=20; p50 1.6 / p95 3.9 ms at t=80); the escalated solve matches the batch-solve runtime (≈30 ms) and is invoked only ahead of interventions.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The fast-path latency is about 0.85ms median and 1.6ms at the 95th percentile on the tested hardware.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: As stated in the text.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Second, at the earliest checkpoint trace length alone is the single best signal (n steps .622 at k=5); OnTrack leads every content- and structure-aware method there but not the length prior — its clearest regime is k=8–10, after the length prior fades and before content accumulates.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Early on, raw trace length alone outpredicts OnTrack, though OnTrack still beats every other content/structure-aware baseline.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: k=5: n steps .622 > OnTrack .612 > LinUOT .595 > cosine .552 (GED .574).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Cell-by-cell check (R3), including a disclosed loss against the length-only baseline.

papers.title: MASS: Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Because the improved model subsequently acts as a better optimizer and evaluator, this alternating framework enables a continuous, recursive bootstrapping of the model's capabilities.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The MASS framework enables continuous, recursive improvement of the model's capabilities across cycles.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Only two cycles were run (L0 -> L1 -> L2). Table 7: Terminal-Bench 2.0 pass rate falls 37.5 -> 35.3 -> 35.2; SWE-bench Verified falls 62.6 -> 61.8 -> 61.1; DSBench is non-monotone (0.473/0.465/0.482). The four research benchmarks do rise (e.g. ScienceAgentBench 28.8 -> 30.4 -> 31.7). Appendix J itself states 'The recursive loop here is empirical... it provides no guarantee that every future cycle improves.' Alternate reading: not_supported, if 'the model's capabilities' is read to include the coding/CLI tasks that actually declined.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss + untested-continuity row (R3 and R5): 'continuous' bootstrapping is tested for only two cycles, and some capability dimensions fall rather than improve.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Moreover, multi-agent traces are also more training-efficient: a student trained on them outperforms a single-agent student trained on 1.4× more training tokens.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: A student trained on multi-agent traces beats a single-agent student trained with 1.4x more tokens.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Numbers match: M+ reaches 68.3% win share at 28.82M processed tokens vs S++ 64.0% at 42.00M (42.00/28.82 = 1.46x; 31.4% fewer tokens; +4.3pp; 50 rollout pairs). But Table 8's own caption says 'M+ has broader training-task coverage and a different sampler, so it is not a matched-data control', and Appendix D.1 notes checkpoint-selection and sampling differences 'limit what can be attributed to teacher composition alone'. The abstract still credits the multi-agent traces unconditionally.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the paper's own caption disclaims the exact matched-control framing the headline sentence implies.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Optimized workflows increasingly place task-specific information in what agents communicate and how they are routed, while reducing redundant information across workflow components.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: As workflows are optimized, agents communicate more task-specific and less redundant information.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Unconditional redundancy TC(Z) falls across all four estimator configurations from iteration 3 to 11. Task-centered TC(Z|T) falls in three configurations but rises for permutation-adjusted MPNet (2.39 -> 2.57, peaking at 2.80 at i=9). Appendix F.3 states the decrease 'concerns the retained path and does not hold for every proposed iterate'; estimates are descriptive statistics from 43-51 agents. Body text hedges ('generally decreases') but the formal Claim 1 box is unhedged.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): one of four estimator configurations for the task-centered redundancy metric does not decrease, contradicting the unhedged formal claim.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Over two MASS cycles with Qwen3.6-27B, the model achieves 1.2–1.6× higher performance per output tokens on four open-ended public benchmarks.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: After two self-improvement cycles, the model is 1.2-1.6x more token-efficient on four open-ended benchmarks.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: MLR-Bench 1.60x, DSBench 1.35x, AstaBench E2E-Hard 1.28x, ScienceAgentBench 1.20x. The sentence is explicitly scoped to these four benchmarks; Terminal-Bench (0.96x) and SWE-bench (0.94x) are shown in the same figure but outside the claim's stated scope.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Verified as scoped; the claim itself only covers the four named benchmarks.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: More directly, M + reaches 68.3% with 28.82M processed supervised tokens, 4.3 points above S++ while using 31.4% fewer tokens.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: M+ beats S++ by 4.3 points while using 31.4% fewer training tokens.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification of the raw numbers (as distinct from the broader framing in P10-R2).

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The agreement increases from 0.73 for L(0) to 0.91 for L(1) and 0.93 for L(2).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Evaluator agreement with ground truth rises steadily across the three self-improvement levels.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: As stated.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Delegation rises from 1/110 trajectories for L(0) to 48/110 for L(1) and 87/110 for L(2), while code handoffs rise from 1/110 to 42/110 and 83/110, respectively.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Delegation and code-handoff behavior both increase sharply across the three self-improvement levels.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: As stated.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Among 114 audited teacher trajectories, 98 contain code handoffs and 57 contain subagent revisions; 79 and 37 of these trajectories, respectively, were sampled for SFT (Appendix G.2).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The audit of 114 teacher trajectories finds widespread code handoffs and subagent revisions, with a subset sampled for SFT.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Recorded 98/57; sampled 79/37.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Multi-agent executions generate approximately 2.4× more tokens on average than single-agent executions and are preferred in 85.1% of external judgments overall.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Multi-agent executions are longer and preferred by external judges most of the time.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Mean generated tokens 141,844 vs 59,355 (ratio 2.39); all pairs 701-123 = 85.1%. Disclosed: equal task weighting instead gives 79.3%.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Numeric verification with a disclosed sensitivity to weighting preserved.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Among the 10 episode pairs with similar generated trace lengths, the multi-agent preference remains 80.0% (Appendix D.3).
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Even controlling for trace length, external judges still prefer multi-agent traces 80% of the time.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Comparable-length subset: 32-8 = 80.0%.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: None of the 180 MLR-Bench executions calls the delegation tool, so this result does not establish delegation as the mechanism of public-benchmark transfer.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Improvement on MLR-Bench is not driven by delegation (which was never invoked), and its statistical significance depends on how results are aggregated.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: 0 of 180 executions call delegation; Welch p=0.0053 and Fisher p=0.0004 for L2 vs L0 at the item level, but a paired sign test over 12 task means gives p=0.2266.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Only the training set is used for Primer synthesis, while all other subsets are reserved for final evaluation; namely, the training and testing sets do not overlap, following the standard machine learning setting.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: UTT's training and test sets never overlap, following standard machine-learning practice.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 1 caption states 'All scores are computed over the full task pool D' (D = D_dist + D_ret + D_frt per Eq. 4, where D_dist is split into a training set used for Primer synthesis and a test set). So the headline numbers (abstract: KernelBench 9.4% -> 48.6%, Omni-MATH-2 27.6% -> 51.7%) include the synthesis training samples. Non-overlapping evaluation is only reported in the split-wise breakdown (Fig. 3, e.g. distillation test set 9.7% -> 64.8%).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Hidden-loss row (R3): the paper's headline numbers are not actually computed on the non-overlapping split the claim describes.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Across the evaluated settings, UTT also outperforms representative prompt engineering and parameter-updating knowledge distillation methods.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: UTT beats both prompt-engineering baselines and parameter-updating knowledge-distillation baselines across all evaluated settings.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Table 2 (prompt-engineering methods) covers Flash and Qwen targets, and UTT wins in all six columns. Table 3 (KD methods: SeqKD, Fine-tune-CoT, RSR, LUFFY) is explicitly titled 'under the Pro->Qwen setting' - KD baselines were never run for a Flash target or with Opus as teacher. UTT does beat the strongest KD baseline there by 7.2, 8.2 and 4 points.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Scope-of-generalization row (R3): the KD comparison only exists for one teacher-student pairing, not 'across the evaluated settings'.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: We observed that the training losses of the KD baselines had largely stabilized by the end of their respective update budgets.

expected_matrix.scoring_notes: No training-loss curve, final loss value, or any convergence metric for SeqKD, Fine-tune-CoT, RSR, or LUFFY appears anywhere in the paper or appendices. This observation is the only support offered for the adequacy of the 100/200-update KD budgets.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested claim (R5): an unmeasured 'we observed' statement is the sole support for a budget-adequacy argument, with no reported metric behind it.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Relative to the unprimed Student baselines, UTT improves KernelBench accuracy from 9.4% to 48.6%, Fast1 from 9% to 35%, and mathematical reasoning accuracy from 27.6% to 51.7%.

papers.title: Hindsight Hierarchies: Learning to Plan by Looking Back

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Our method is inspired by the following asymmetry in problem solving: It is, in general, harder to solve a problem from scratch than to reverse engineer the idea underlying a known solution.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: It is generally harder to solve a problem from scratch than to reverse-engineer the idea behind a known solution.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: No experiment, measurement, or citation supports this asymmetry anywhere in the paper. Section 6 calls it 'our central hypothesis' and adds 'it is a priori not clear that solution ideas derived in hindsight are suitable targets for foresight prediction. This highlights the need for a thorough experimental evaluation.' Alternate reading: this is background intuition used as motivation, not a result claim. Shares evidence/premise with P12-R2.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested foundational premise (R5): the paper itself labels this a hypothesis needing future experimental evaluation.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: For a reasoning model, this presents a learning opportunity: even when a problem exceeds its current solving abilities, a supplied solution may enable it to extract a useful idea for solving that problem in hindsight.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: Supplying a solution lets the model extract a useful idea in hindsight, which can then supervise learning to find that idea unaided.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: The paper runs no experiments: no generated hindsight ideas are evaluated, no training loop is run, no comparison with standard supervised fine-tuning. Section 6: 'a high score does not by itself establish that the retained idea helped the model solve the problem' and 'Future work should experimentally evaluate the proposed method.' Hedges ('might', 'may', 'can') narrow scope but do not rescue a never-tested claim. Shares evidence with P12-R1 (treat the pair as about 1.5 independent rows). Related sentences (not the claim): Such a reconstructed idea can then provide additional supervision for learning to develop a solution idea from the problem alone, before attempting to solve it. (p.1); The opportunity is therefore to learn from ideas that the model can already reverse engineer, but may not yet be able to discover unaided. (p.1).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Untested foundational premise (R1 and R5): hedging words do not rescue a mechanism the paper explicitly says still needs experimental evaluation.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: We give a formal specification of our method and a concrete instantiation for interactive theorem proving in the Lean theorem prover; empirical evaluation remains future work.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The paper is a method specification with a Lean instantiation and explicitly reports no empirical results.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: The paper contains a formal specification (Sections 3-5) and Lean instantiation (Section 5, Appendix A), and no benchmark results. Related sentences (not the claim): This version of the manuscript reports no empirical evaluation. (p.13).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: The paper's own self-description, verified against its contents.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The example texts are hand-written illustrations, not model outputs or empirical observations.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The example texts used to illustrate the method are hand-written, not generated by a model.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: As stated in the figure caption.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Importantly, the teacher is only used for the generation of the seed dataset, i.e., does not appear in the subsequent training loop, where hindsight hierarchies are exclusively generated by the hindsight component.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: After the initial seed dataset, the hindsight component (not the teacher model) generates all subsequent hindsight hierarchies.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Algorithm 1: iterations after the seed use only H_theta.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Specification verified against the described algorithm.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Consequently, every triple returned by Algorithm 2 contains a valid solution discovered by the solver under the triple's hierarchy.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: By construction, Algorithm 2 only returns triples that include a verified valid solution.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Algorithm 2 only returns a triple when the score meets the acceptance threshold delta > 0, which requires at least one successful verified solver run.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Logical consequence of the stated algorithm, not an empirical claim.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: All three components are implemented using a single underlying language model with shared parameters, and we distinguish between components using role-specific prompt templates.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The solver, foresight, and hindsight components all share one underlying model and parameter set.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Shared model internlm/internlm2-math-plus-7b; 'All trainable parameters are shared; prompts distinguish components.'

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Thus, each mini-batch contains a total of b = bS + (n + 1)(bF + bH) prompt-response pairs.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The paper gives a formula for mini-batch composition in terms of solver, foresight, and hindsight sample counts.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: bS solver pairs plus bF per foresight group plus bH per hindsight group, with n+1 groups each.
expected_matrix.why_this_case: Formula verified against the source text.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: The concrete prompt templates in Appendix A.3 use two levels (n = 1): a detailed plan z0 and a coarse proof idea z1; neither is required to consist of executable Lean commands.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The Lean instantiation uses exactly two hierarchy levels: a detailed plan and a coarser idea.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: z0 = DETAILED PLAN, z1 = COARSE IDEA.

expected_matrix.claim_text_verbatim: Nevertheless, it is a priori not clear that solution ideas derived in hindsight are suitable targets for foresight prediction.
expected_matrix.claim_summary: The paper's own discussion section names the specific experimental gaps future work needs to fill.
expected_matrix.scoring_notes: Quoted text, verified verbatim against the source. Related sentences (not the claim): The evaluation should cover both the Lean instantiation and the version without a verifier, and include comparisons with standard supervised fine-tuning under comparable data and computational budgets, as well as thorough ablation studies. (p.13).
expected_matrix.why_this_case: The paper's own stated limitations, verified against the source.
